data.title: Dreveník – a Slavic hillfort in the shadow of Spiš Castle
data.excerpt: In the Hornád Basin south-east of Spišské Podhradie rises Dreveník, the largest travertine mound in Slovakia — a unique rock city whose levelled summit plateau, ringed by faces up to 60 m high, was used for defence in almost every historical period. children.text: We present another interesting Slavic hillfort from eastern Slovakia.

In the Hornád Basin, south-east of the town of Spišské Podhradie, lies the largest travertine mound in Slovakia, a unique natural formation with a rock city, of at least central European significance. The summit plateau represented an exceptional position, used for defensive purposes in almost all historical periods. The most pronounced building activity dates from the 9th–11th century, when a Slavic hillfort stood there; after its timber fortification and dwelling structures the area was named Dreveník.

children.text: From the end of the Tertiary, tectonic faults have brought water enriched with calcium bicarbonate up to limestones overlain by conglomerates and claystones. Through its sedimentation from the warm mineral springs, with the combined action of pressure, temperature and climate, travertine layers were laid down in characteristic mounds. Compared with the other mounds (Pažica or Sivá Brada), Dreveník was more heavily broken up by mechanical action, which gave rise to rock towers, caves, fissures and the like. The edges of Dreveník thus form steep, mostly vertical faces up to 60 m high. The top of the mound was at the same time levelled off, resulting in an all but perfect space for shelter, or for the construction of defensive works. From this impregnable place, considerably elevated above its surroundings, there was also an excellent view over the whole basin. Even if an enemy had taken the extensive summit plateau with its perfect potential for building dwelling structures, there was still a fallback possibility of shelter in the cave systems.

children.text: It is no surprise, then, that the earliest occupation dates as far back as the Palaeolithic (finds of

) and the Neolithic (the Bükk culture). The first fortification was built there in the Eneolithic (the Baden culture), on which further cultures of the Bronze Age and certainly also of the Iron Age then followed. The most pronounced occupation dates from the 9th–11th century, when the extensive plateau was used as a refuge. The Early Middle Ages were a relatively restless period and danger often threatened. Dreveník was therefore a very suitable place of shelter for the local Slavic population, which built dwellings and later also defensive works on the plateau. The first incorporation of the hillfort, or refuge, into an organised defensive system may be assumed under the rule of Svatopluk I (871–894), when Great Moravia expanded as far as the middle course of the Hornád. The period between the demise of Great Moravia and the joining of this territory to the Kingdom of Hungary was again unstable and restless, as is shown by the finds from the 10th–11th century, which are the most numerous. With the emergence of the county system and of other centres of administration, but above all with the calming of the political situation, the hillfort came to an end in the course of the 12th century. It may, however, have been used again during the Mongol invasion, as finds from the 13th century also show.
A few photographs from Svätoháj rodnej viery:
The present state of the site

At present the site of the main hillfort lies in the cadastral area of Spišské Podhradie, on the boundary of the cadastral area of Žehra. It is the south-western spur of the central part of Dreveník (560–570 m above sea level), where the site is bounded by rock precipices and, on the north-east, by a preserved massive rampart bank. The earth-and-stone rampart runs NW–SSE, its length is 60 m and its height in places as much as 2 m. Over the last thousand years it has been considerably destroyed by natural processes, so its original height was at least twice the present one. Various finds from the site attest the function of the hillfort in the 9th–11th century. Investigations were carried out there as early as 1932 by J. Neustupný, then by V. Budinský-Krička, V. Furmánek and M. Slivka.
